challenges.evidence: Byte-spliced word 1 of each cry verse (verse_map_oshb.json, collate byte tier at its own ref): oshb:Ps.107.6 = וַיִּצְעֲק֣וּ ; oshb:Ps.107.13 = וַיִּזְעֲק֣וּ ; oshb:Ps.107.19 = וַיִּזְעֲק֣וּ ; oshb:Ps.107.28 = וַיִּצְעֲק֣וּ . The seam warrant for 107:10 does not depend on the claim, so the cure is a re-cut sentence, but the claim as written is a positive false statement about the original-language distribution and it contradicts the byte-accurate tsade-zayin-zayin-tsade description carried elsewhere in the same psalm's rows.

reviews.reasoning: Every OL claim re-derived clean. The cry quote collates at byte tier against oshb:Ps.107.19 and its 4-word clause is byte-identical to MT 107:13 (2 of 4 cry verses), so 'matching the prisoners' company's cry' is exact and the contrast with the tsade spelling of MT 107:6 is byte-true. The yodu slice collates at byte tier against oshb:Ps.107.21, whose whole verse is byte-identical to MT 107:8, 107:15 and 107:31 (4 of 4 verses). The inverted-nun disclosure matches pmarks_Ps.json exactly: the reversednun object holds 7 keys (oshb:Ps.107.20, .21, .22, .23, .24, .25, .39), one seg each, so '3 of the book's 7' for this span is right, and the row correctly labels them seg layer, single-witness, not quotable as verse bytes - it never uses them as a driver. The contrast the rationale draws for 107:22 is byte-supported: MT 107:9 and MT 107:16 both open with verse-initial ki (3 of 43 verses in the psalm, skeleton tier on word 1) while MT 107:22 opens with a waw-prefixed verb, so 'sacrifice and song rather than the plain motive clause' is a real form difference, not taste. unit_type refrain_unit is inside the controlled vocabulary and confidence high is carried by the refrain bytes. Observation only, not filed: check_universals raises a WARN on rejected_alternative's phrase about 107:22 carrying no cry-refrain of its own, which has no adjacent digit; the claim is single-verse and span-scoped rather than a corpus universal, and it is byte-true (0 of the 4 cry-refrain openers falls at MT 107:22).

The outer edges of 107:23-32 are byte-hard and I do not contest the span: the cry quote collates at byte tier against oshb:Ps.107.28 and its clause is byte-identical to MT 107:6, the yodu slice collates at byte tier against oshb:Ps.107.31 whose whole verse is byte-identical to MT 107:8, 107:15 and 107:21 (4 of 4 verses), and the row's tsade-zayin-zayin-tsade description of the four cries is exactly what the spliced openers show. The 10-verse length is governed by the refrain-return rule for refrained psalms rather than the 4-8 verse strophe guidance, and rejected_alternative engages the 27|28 rival honestly. The inverted-nun refs match pmarks_Ps.json (oshb:Ps.107.23, .24, .25 are three of the seven keys). Two defects are filed: one factual claim about MT 107:25 that the bytes refute, and a register-plus-count defect in the inverted-nun bookkeeping.

challenges.claim: The continuity warrant for 24|25 rests on a syntactic description that is false of the Hebrew - MT 107:25 does not open with a causal clause but with a waw-prefixed narrative form, and no original language is quoted for the claim.
challenges.evidence: Byte-spliced word 1 of oshb:Ps.107.25 = וַיֹּ֗אמֶר (waw-prefixed prefix-conjugation form; the full verse collates at byte tier and the row cites oshb:Ps.107.25 only as an inverted-nun seg, quoting no Hebrew for the syntax claim). Verse-initial ki in Ps 107 occurs in 3 of 43 verses (skeleton tier, word-1 comparison) - MT 107:9, MT 107:11, MT 107:16 - and MT 107:25 is not among them; the ki token spliced from oshb:Ps.107.9 word 1 is כִּי . The causal reading enters only through the WEB rendering the row quotes immediately before the claim, “For he commands, and raises the stormy wind, which lifts up its waves.” (web:Ps.107.25), where 'For' is a translator's supply with no counterpart in the quoted bytes; the row's own words are 'verse 25 opens with a causal clause continuing 107:24's wonders, so no seam separates the setting from the storm', which makes the English artifact carry a boundary warrant. The continuity conclusion is recoverable from the bytes - the waw prefix is itself a continuation signal - so this is a warrant defect, not a span defect, and the replacement must be argued from oshb:Ps.107.25 rather than from web:Ps.107.25.

challenges.claim: The row breaches three separate classes of the standing register purge - a strategy-file citation, a positional row reference, and writer meta-narration - and the positional reference also outsources this row's own closing-seam warrant to another row.
challenges.evidence: rejected_alternative reads 'Reading 107:33-43 as one eleven-verse coda was considered, and aligns with the strategy's own framing of one wisdom-coda; this writer agrees in part, splitting it instead at 107:38|39 -- see the next row's rationale for the internal seam argued there.' device_notes adds 'argued honestly here rather than assumed: this writer splits it at 107:38|39'. TOOLKIT.md standing rules and the book strategy's register section both forbid, in row prose EVER: strategy-file/section citations ('the strategy's own framing'), positional row references ('see the next row's rationale'), and review-actor or process naming ('this writer', 'argued honestly here'); cross-row references must be verse-anchored, e.g. the seam at 107:38|39. The substantive cost is not cosmetic: of the row's 2 outer seams, 1 (the closing edge at 107:38|39) has no byte evidence stated anywhere in the row, and rejected_alternative discharges it by pointing at another row rather than by carrying a warrant, so the register cure and the seam-pair warrant have to be authored together on both rows.

challenges.claim: Quote/gloss desync at oshb:Ps.107.39: the gloss covers only the first of the two quoted Hebrew words and imports an adverb that has no lexical counterpart in the quoted span.
challenges.evidence: The row quotes 2 words, byte-spliced and byte tier at its cited ref: וַיִּמְעֲט֥וּ וַיָּשֹׁ֑חוּ (oshb:Ps.107.39), and glosses them 'again, they are diminished'. The second word, וַיָּשֹׁ֑חוּ , is rendered in the other witness as and bowed down and is left uncovered by the gloss, while 'again' corresponds to no token in the quoted span - it enters from the WEB rendering “Again, they are diminished and bowed down through oppression, trouble, and sorrow.” (web:Ps.107.39), where it translates the waw prefix. The standing rule is that quote spans and their glosses cover the SAME span and that parity repairs re-cut the gloss rather than truncate the Hebrew; here the correct repair is to extend the gloss to both words and to drop the imported adverb, since observed_substrate_signals then rests the row's pivot on 'again' as well - it calls the 2-word quote a reversal-opening token, singular, on the strength of the same English adverb.

challenges.claim: A byte-true form signal straddles this row's opening seam undisclosed: the waw-prefixed narrative chain runs unbroken from MT 107:36 through MT 107:39, so the strongest form-class break in the neighbourhood falls at 39|40, the rival seam the row rejects without engaging that evidence.

MT 107:40 = שֹׁפֵ֣ךְ is the single opener in MT 107:36-41 that carries no waw prefix (1 of 6 verses). The row's warrant for opening at 107:39 is the semantic reversal, marked in the other witness by “Again,” at the head of “Again, they are diminished and bowed down through oppression, trouble, and sorrow.” (web:Ps.107.39); no Hebrew form evidence is offered for the seam, and the unbroken 36-39 chain that argues continuity against it is not disclosed. Under the standing cross-seam cohesion rule a byte-true device straddling a row's own seam argues continuity against the row unless disclosed. I do not assert the span is wrong - MT 107:41 resumes a waw-prefixed opener, so 107:40 is an isolated break rather than the head of a new chain, and the semantic pivot at 107:39 is real - but rejected_alternative rejects the 107:40-43 rival without touching the one byte-visible form datum in the neighbourhood, and the straddle must be disclosed on both rows of the 38|39 seam pair in one edit.
